Task: Outline and partially script a 15-minute educational video on climate change.

15-Minute Educational Video on Climate Change  
Target: General audience (ages 14 +, no prior science background)  
Working Title: “Climate Change: The Story of Our Changing Planet”

––––––––––––––––––––––  
HIGH-LEVEL OUTLINE (15:00)

0:00–1:00 Cold-open hook  
1:00–4:00 Segment 1 – What Is Climate Change?  
4:00–7:00 Segment 2 – Proof: How We Know It’s Real  
7:00–9:00 Segment 3 – The Human Fingerprint (Causes)  
9:00–12:00 Segment 4 – Impacts Happening Now  
12:00–14:00 Segment 5 – Solutions & Hope  
14:00–15:00 Closing, Call-to-Action & Credits  

Learning Objectives  
• Define climate vs. weather and climate change vs. global warming.  
• Recognize at least three lines of scientific evidence for modern climate change.  
• Identify the main anthropogenic drivers (CO₂, CH₄, deforestation, etc.).  
• Describe three current or projected impacts on people and ecosystems.  
• List individual, community, and policy solutions that curb warming.

––––––––––––––––––––––  
DETAILED BEAT SHEET & PARTIAL SCRIPT

NOTE: “Host” refers to the on-camera presenter. “VO” = voice-over. Scene & graphic suggestions appear in brackets. Feel free to shorten or expand lines during production.

0:00–1:00 – COLD-OPEN HOOK  
[Visual: Drone shot rising over wildfire-scarred hillside → smash-cut to flooded city street → time-lapse of melting glacier → upbeat music fades in.]  
HOST (on-location, city rooftop at sunrise):  
“Wildfires in California, floods in Germany, record heat in India—different stories…one common thread. In the next 15 minutes we’ll unpack the science of climate change, see its fingerprints across the globe, and explore what you and I can do—today—to rewrite the ending.”

TITLE CARD (05 s)  
Text: “Climate Change: The Story of Our Changing Planet”

1:00–4:00 – SEGMENT 1: WHAT IS CLIMATE CHANGE?  
1:00–1:45  
[Graphic: Animated globe showing 30-year average temps vs. daily weather blips.]  
HOST:  
“First things first: Weather is what you get day-to-day—rain, shine, snow. Climate is the long-term average of that weather…30 years or more. Climate change means those long-term patterns are shifting.”

1:45–2:45  
[Graphic: ‘Keeling Curve’ plot appears; CO₂ parts per million rising.]  
VO:  
“Since the Industrial Revolution, global average temperature has risen about 1.2 °C (2 °F). That might sound small, but across an entire planet it’s huge—like turning up a global thermostat.”

2:45–4:00  
[Interactive street interview montage — quick vox-pops where people guess causes, impacts.]  
HOST (wrap-up):  
“So why is this happening? Let’s follow the evidence.”

4:00–7:00 – SEGMENT 2: PROOF – HOW WE KNOW IT’S REAL  
4:00–5:00  
[Graphic: NASA 140-year anomaly map animation.]  
HOST:  
“Thousands of thermometers worldwide tell the same story—rapid warming, especially since the 1970s.”

5:00–5:45  
[Visual: Ice core drilling in Antarctica.]  
VO:  
“Ice cores preserve ancient air bubbles. They show today’s CO₂ levels haven’t been this high in at least 800,000 years.”

5:45–6:15  
[Graphic: Sea-level gauge animation.]  
HOST:  
“Oceans are also testimony: they’ve risen 20 cm (8 in) in the past century as ice melts and water expands.”

6:15–7:00  
[Side-by-side split screen: Flower bloom dates 1950 vs. today; polar bear on shrinking ice.]  
HOST (to camera):  
“When plants bloom earlier and glaciers vanish, it’s like nature leaving post-it notes for us: ‘Things are changing!’”

7:00–9:00 – SEGMENT 3: THE HUMAN FINGERPRINT (CAUSES)  
7:00–7:45  
[Visual: Chimney stacks; overlay pie chart of greenhouse gases.]  
HOST:  
“Greenhouse gases trap heat—CO₂ is biggest, methane second. Burning coal, oil, and gas adds ~37 billion tonnes of CO₂ each year.”

7:45–8:30  
[Graphic: Correlation line—fossil-fuel emissions vs. temperature rise.]  
VO:  
“Computer models match observed warming only when human emissions are included. Natural factors alone can’t explain it.”

8:30–9:00  
[Scene: Host at kitchen table with clear jar, lamp, thermometer; quick DIY greenhouse demo.]  
HOST:  
“Even at home you can recreate the effect: more CO₂, higher temperature. Scale it up—planet-size—and you see the challenge.”

9:00–12:00 – SEGMENT 4: IMPACTS HAPPENING NOW  
9:00–9:45  
[Footage: Hurricane aftermath; graphic overlay of trend lines in storm intensity.]  
HOST:  
“Warmer oceans turbocharge storms—like super-filling a fuel tank.”

9:45–10:30  
[Visual: Small-holder farmer in Kenya; dried cracked soil.]  
VO:  
“Droughts threaten crops and water security, pushing communities toward food scarcity.”

10:30–11:15  
[Scene: Coral reef bleaching time-lapse.]  
HOST:  
“Oceans absorb 90 % of excess heat. Corals—home to 25 % of marine species—are bleaching under the stress.”

11:15–12:00  
[Graphic: Global climate-migration map animation.]  
VO:  
“By 2050, climate could displace up to 216 million people—roughly two-thirds the U.S. population.”

12:00–14:00 – SEGMENT 5: SOLUTIONS & HOPE  
12:00–12:40  
[Montage: Solar farm, offshore wind, rooftop panels.]  
HOST:  
“Clean energy is booming. Solar costs dropped 89 % since 2010, and renewables now supply nearly 30 % of global power.”

12:40–13:20  
[Visual: City bike lanes, electric buses, plant-based burger.]  
VO:  
“Solutions span energy, transport, food, and forests. Each choice cuts emissions and creates jobs.”

13:20–14:00  
[Scene: Classroom with students building climate sensors.]  
HOST (to camera):  
“We need systemic policy shifts—but personal actions build momentum. Vote, innovate, educate, and collaborate.”

14:00–15:00 – CLOSING & CALL-TO-ACTION  
14:00–14:30  
HOST (sunset on rooftop):  
“Climate change is human-caused, but that means the future is human-chosen. The chapters ahead are still unwritten.”

14:30–14:50  
ON-SCREEN TEXT & VO:  
“Learn more: IPCC.ch | NASA Climate | Project Drawdown  
Take action: Fridays for Future | The U.S. Inflation Reduction Act incentives | Local climate groups.”

14:50–15:00  
ROLL CREDITS over upbeat music & montage of hopeful images (tree-planting, community solar ribbon-cutting, youth climate march).

––––––––––––––––––––––  
PRODUCTION NOTES

Visual Style  
• Mix cinematic b-roll with motion graphics.  
• Color palette: Warm oranges for impacts, cool blues/greens for solutions.  
• On-screen captions for key stats; QR codes link to deeper resources.

Interactive Elements (optional)  
• Pause point at 6:15: pop-quiz overlay (“Name two lines of evidence for climate change.”).  
• Poll card at 12:30: “Which sector do you think emits most greenhouse gases worldwide?”

Accessibility  
• Closed captions.  
• Audio descriptions for critical visuals.  
• Color-blind-friendly palettes for graphs.

––––––––––––––––––––––  
RESOURCE LIST FOR FURTHER READING (for video description box)

1. IPCC Sixth Assessment Report – Summary for Policymakers  
2. NASA Global Climate Change: Vital Signs  
3. Project Drawdown Solutions Library  
4. U.S. NOAA Climate.gov Teaching Resources  
5. “Speed & Scale” by John Doerr – for policy & tech roadmaps

––––––––––––––––––––––  
END
